en: Biography of the Great Virtuous One, the Three Court Attendant of Daqingshansi during the Three Tang Dynasties:
The late Master’s name was Huiguo. His secular surname was Ma, and he was a native of Guiming Township, Wannian County, Jingzhao Prefecture.
At the young age of nine, he entered the Shengfo Monastery; thus, he served as the National Preceptor for the Inner Sanctuary throughout the three reigns. He maintained...
I call to mind the Purple-Robed Śramaṇa, the Venerable Master named Tanzhen. He resolved to study the sūtras and reached the age of seventeen.

Serving as an attendant to the Venerable Master, he constantly remained within the Inner Court of the Dharma, reciting mantras without leaving. He then [sought instruction] from the Tripiṭaka Master at Xingshan Temple.

At the age of nineteen, he requested the transmission of the *Mahāpratisarā* and other dhāraṇīs from the Tripiṭaka Master. The Master performed the empowerment (*abhiṣeka*) and the rite of scattering flowers (*puṣpa-prakiraṇa*).
He obtained the Bodhisattva Dharmacakra-vartana. The Upādhyāya said: "In the land of South India, I scattered flowers and obtained this Honored One;
it is no different from now. After my passing, you shall propagate and transmit the Great Teaching of the Total-Holders (*dhāraṇī*), no different from myself."
Furthermore, in the third month of the eighth year of the Dali era, an imperial edict was issued to establish a Vaipulya (fangdeng) ritual site at Ci’en Monastery.
The Venerable Preceptor of the Shengfo Yuan, having received the edict from Ci’en Monastery to establish the Vaipulya ritual site, reports:

"I have two young novices who are twenty years of age and capable of receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*). However, I have not yet dared to unilaterally grant them the tonsure and ordain them. I prostrate myself.

I beg for Your Majesty’s compassionate favor to permit this servant to return to the monastery with the two youths, and to grant them their precept robes and alms bowls. May Your Majesty also deign to bestow one ceremonial sword;
before the Great Buddha Hall of Qinglong Monastery, I shall confer these imperial edicts upon the Upādhyāya and the two youths to have their heads shaved.

Furthermore, may two sets each of kaṣāyas, robes, and alms bowls be granted, along with official decrees for their ordination and residency at the monastery. May the Imperial Messenger escort the Upādhyāya to Cien Monastery.

The ceremony at the temple concluded. He then entered the palace to express his gratitude for the Imperial Edict. The humble monk [name] humbly thanks Your Majesty’s sacred compassion for granting two youths ordination and providing them with robes, alms bowls, and razors.
Furthermore, the official decree and the imperial messenger were sent to the ritual arena of Ci’en Temple to bestow the precepts.
Having completed the conferral of the precepts, this humble monk cannot contain his joy and prostrates himself in celebration. At the age of twenty-two, he again, at [the temple of] Wu...

He sought the transmission of the Great Yoga of the Mahāyoga of Vairocana from the Great Compassion Womb (Mahāvairocanābhisambodhi), as well as the Mahāyoga of Susiddhi and the various *yoga* methods for the various deities, from the Upādhyāya Xuanchao, who was a disciple of the Tripiṭaka Master.
Each of these he received through the Master’s personal instruction. Furthermore, he sought [these teachings] from the Tripiṭaka Master at Daxingshan Temple.

He was granted the *Vajraśekhara-mahāyogatantra-rāja-dharma* and the secret mudrās of the various deities' yoga, having received direct instruction from his former master regarding what he had obtained within.
As a token of the grace of being conferred this dharma, he presented a letter to the Tripitaka Master.
Whenever he was beneath the pavilion, he would restrict his food and set a time limit, reciting it several times during each session. At the age of twenty...
5. He was specially granted an imperial decree by the Emperor’s grace to enter the palace. At that time, while at Changsheng Hall, he was summoned by an edict and questioned:
"What efficacious powers do you possess? Jia Tian replied, "This humble monk has no great efficacy.

Thereupon, by imperial command, eight youths were summoned to perform the ritual of *kǎozhào* (summoning spirits) and receive empowerment; whatever the Emperor commanded them to accomplish, they all achieved success. The record was then transcribed.
The bamboo joints joined together with the vase, and success was achieved. The Emperor was greatly pleased.

In the tenth year of the Dali era, he issued a special imperial edict to grant one East Pagoda Courtyard at this very temple, establishing a Vairocana Consecration Mandala there, where seven monks were to maintain the recitations.
In the eleventh year of the Dali era, he performed empowerment for Emperor Daizong, and the illness was cured immediately. Imperial Edict.

A pair of purple robes was bestowed [upon him]. He submitted a memorial stating that he did not dare accept them, and returned them immediately. The Imperial Edict stated: "I have already bestowed the purple robes upon you, Master;
why do you refuse to accept them? He replied: "I am but a humble monk of this realm. To be granted purple robes would be an honor too great for me to bear; I ought indeed to accept them at once.
However, my Preceptor received the purple robes from the late Emperor, and as a disciple, it is not fitting for me to be on equal footing with my Master. The Emperor said:

"The Master is most filial; this was my own error. The Imperial Edict stated: "Among those of other lineages and different surnames, you alone maintain a heart of reverence, obedience, and filial piety.
From this day forward, you shall serve as National Preceptor. Thereupon, he was granted a pair of coarse cloth robes (*khaṭvāṅga*) and received the empowerment of the Imperial Edict.
Princess Hwayang recovered from her illness within three days. Later, during the *shen* and *wei* hours, the Princess suddenly...
[The Emperor] spoke. The Emperor and the palace ladies all stepped forward together. The Preceptor addressed him, saying: "It is currently hot;

I hope that Your Majesty will allow the palace ladies to come before me for a moment so that this humble monk may perform a consecration (*adhiṣṭhāna*), whereby they shall immediately be cured. The Princess was then cured, her speech becoming clear once more.
The Emperor was greatly pleased and bestowed upon him one hundred rolls of silk and a pair of robes. [The Preceptor] thanked the Imperial Decree, saying: "I, your servant..."

The *kṣatriya* [monk] [name] expresses his gratitude for the Imperial Grace bestowed of silk and robes; he cannot sufficiently express his prostrations of joy. (On the third day, it was orally reported that the Princess was being moved.
During the Dali era, all the money and goods granted as imperial favors, totaling over one thousand strings of cash, were entirely used to cultivate merit beneath the stupa.

In the thirteenth year of the Dali era, he petitioned twice, both before and after, to tour the Southern Terrace. In accordance with the Master’s petition, the Upādhyāya [performed rites] at the Observatory...
At the Sound Terrace, while engaged in recitation for a long duration of the night, the Great Sage Avalokiteśvara manifested a great physical form within a great lunar disc.
His radiance was like that of the midday sun, and auspicious clouds were pure and bright. Simultaneously, several hundred thousand people from afar joined in gazing upon and prostrating to him.

In the thirteenth year of the Dali era, an imperial edict was issued for the transmission of the Dharma and the conferral of empowerment (abhiṣeka) at the inner chapel of the Changsheng Hall during the three morning audiences.

Upon the passing of the Tripiṭaka Master Upādhyāya, an imperial edict was issued to Huiguo, stating: "After the Tripiṭaka Master Upādhyāya has passed away, there shall be no time when the Buddha-dharma is left without a successor.
Hearing that you, Master, have mastered the Great Dharma, we entrust the entirety of the state's affairs to you, following in the footsteps of the late Upādhyāya."

He was granted the dharma-gate of the method for recitation, yet he frequently forgot it. On another day, when [the Emperor] summoned him and questioned him about it, this was equivalent to the rank of Master.
On the fifteenth day of the tenth month in the thirteenth year of the Dali era, Gao Li Xiancheng proclaimed.

At the beginning of the Jianzhong era, there was a monk named Bianhong from the Kingdom of □□, who brought a set of bronze cymbals from his own country and offered them to the Shengfo Monastery, along with a conch shell.
Two sets [of robes]. Four copper *kundi* jars. [These] were offered to the Upādhyāya to serve as offerings, seeking the transmission of the Great Dharma of the Womb Realm (*garbhadhātu*) Vairocana.

In the second year of the Jianzhong era, the Silla monk Hye-il presented tribute from his own country to the Upādhyāya, seeking the transmission of the Womb Realm, the Vajradhātu, the Susiddhi, and the various deities' yogas. III.

Having received and mastered these ten volumes, he later returned to his native country, where he widely propagated the Great Teaching. Through his sincere devotion, he abstained from grain while maintaining his recitations;
siddhi manifested before him, and he eventually ascended into the heavens during broad daylight. The king of that land came to the palace to gaze upon and pay homage to him.
He sought this Dharma. In the air, a voice spoke, saying: "In the Great Tang country to the west, there is a secret Dharma;

within that Dharma, there is Qinglong Monastery. In the same year, a monk from Silla named Wuzhen was granted the teachings for the visualization and recitation of the Vairocana of the Womb Realm (*garbhadhātu*) and its various deities.
In the fifth year of the Zhenyuan era, he traveled to Central India to [seek] Vairocana.
Regarding the remaining scriptures of the *Vajraśekhara* cycle, [the Master] passed away in the country of T'u-fan (Tibet).

His disciples at this monastery, the monks Gishō, Gumon, and Jitchō, simultaneously requested from their Upādhyāya the transmission of thirty scriptural texts, including the *Vairocanābhisambodhi*, the *Garbhadhātu*, and the *Susiddhi*.
In the fifth year of the Chengyuan era, by imperial decree, they were ordered to perform prayers before the Great Buddha Hall of this temple with seven monks.
It rained. On the night of the seventh day, the rain was sufficient. To each [monk] he granted one bundle of silk and ten strings of tea as a token of thanks.
By imperial decree, [the image] was escorted by the Right Guard to have its true body (śarīra) brought into the palace.

On the □ day of the fourth month in the sixth year of the Zhenyuan era, it was decreed that the monk Huiguo be ordered to enter the palace to perform recitations for the sake of the state in the Changsheng Hall. He remained within the palace for more than seventy days.

They were released and returned home. Each was granted thirty bolts of silk and twenty bundles of tea. Thereafter, they were assigned to alternating shifts between upper and lower ranks and were bestowed with seasonal clothing and provisions for the three festivals.
At that time, Prime Minister Du Huang-chang and Prime Minister Wei personally stated that they had received the *abhiṣeka* (consecration) and studied the recitation [of mantras].

They petitioned once more to request a tour of inspection of the temple precincts; by imperial decree, it was ordered that their request be granted, and they were appointed as Great Virtuous Monks (*bhadanta*) of Guanyin Temple.

From the ninth year of the Zhenyuan era to the thirteenth year, there were Yi-heng, Yi-yi, Yi-zheng, Yi-□, Yi-cao, Yi-yun, Zhi-xing, Yi-min, Xing-jian, Yuan-tong, Yi-lun, Yi-bo, and Yi-run; as well as the lay disciple Wu Yin.
Kaipei and others, numbering approximately fifty, were studying the Dharma. In the fifth month of the fourteenth year of the Zhenyuan era, there was a great drought.

During the first ten days of the fifth month, by imperial decree, they were commissioned to pray for rain. For seven days, they remained within the Inner Sanctuary, single-mindedly maintaining their recitations.

When the days of the rain-prayer were completed, the Emperor graciously bestowed one bundle of silk and ten strings of tea. In gratitude, we, the monk-subjects, acknowledge that we have sought merit through our practice, and thus Heaven has sent down its bounty.
A sweet rain has fallen; the Emperor’s transformative influence is profound. We monks offer our thanks for the silk and tea, and we cannot sufficiently express our supreme gratitude.
In the late eighth month of the fifteenth year of the Zhenyuan era, the Empress Dowager performed *kaji* (empowerment) for the Crown Prince, who recovered after three days.
Each was granted twenty bolts of silk, fifty bolts of Wu-ling silk, and twenty bundles of tea. We, humble monks of this realm, thank the Imperial Benevolence for bestowing this silk and cloth.

Tea. I cannot sufficiently express my congratulations. On the sixteenth day of the eleventh month of winter in the sixteenth year, the soldiers Jiao and Hu of the Shenwei Army invited the Venerable Master to their military quarters for an offering, and presented the Venerable Master’s portrait, which had been decorated and sent to the monastery. In the eighteenth year.

The Upādhyāya’s clan attained increasing prominence. He submitted a memorial requesting his retirement, and by imperial decree was granted leave to return home, being ordered to recuperate at the monastery for the time being.
It was my intention that he remain until the end of his life, but Zhan was unable to comply.

In the middle of the eighth month of that year, he relinquished his robes and bowl, entrusting them to seven individuals, including Yiming, for their use. In the nineteenth year of the Zhenguan era, the Japanese monk Kūkai [received them].
By imperial decree, he was provided with a *mona* (patchwork robe) and over five hundred strings of currency as national tribute.

He offered these all to the Upādhyāya, dedicating them entirely to the adornment of the ritual site (*maṇḍala*) and making offerings. He requested the transmission of the *Mahākaruṇā-garbha-vajradhātu* and the various yoga teachings of the deities.
Within fifty days, he beheld the realm of the *Brahmā-akṣara* (the letter A), the sun and moon disks, which appeared and entered his mouth.
In the middle [of the year], on the fifth day of the eighth month of the twenty-first year of the Zhenyuan era, the reign title was changed to the first year of Yongzhen.
On the fifteenth day of the twelfth month, he was interred with his head facing north.

On the seventeenth day of the first month of the first year of the Yuanhe era, approximately one thousand disciples, both monastic and lay, escorted his funeral procession to the side of the Great Master’s stupa at Longyuan in Mengcun. Thereafter, until the Baoli era...
On the twenty-first day of the eighth month of the second year [of the Huichang era], Yiyi, Shenda, and Yidan erected a stupa and relocated the burial by the side of the San River at Liaocun.
On the thirteenth day of the first month of the fourth year of the Kaicheng era, the Japanese monk Enkyō [arrived].
The dharma robe and sacred objects were entrusted [to him].
(A note on the manuscript states:
Completed at the hour of Xu on the twenty-fifth day of the eighth month in the first year of Jōan (the Great Age *Xinmao*).

On the final day of the ninth month in the first year of Kanshō (1320), having completed the transcription at the monastic quarters of Saikoin in Tōji, this was written as a complete copy for the sake of [the] *Chū*...
[text missing]. (Nakagawa Hon'ya)
The Great Dharma Master Vajrarāmaṇi.
